comments.name: D E Kuppler

WASHINGTON, Oct. 4, 1940 — President Roosevelt said Friday his administration reached an agreement for Nazi Germany to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of heating oil, easing pressure on Berlin over its bombing of Britain in hopes of lowering fuel prices before the November election.

The move suspends oil sanctions on German exports for six months. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, &Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Roosevelt said.

Just last month he signed a bipartisan measure to squeeze importers of German oil. Prime Minister Churchill warned that easing sanctions "is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged." 

Sen. Vandenberg said he feared the deal would "only fund the Nazi war machine."But German oil is cheap, & Washington calls that a bargain. The Reich's envoy Ribbentrop praised the deal: "German-American cooperation on oil and energy will benefit the world.

2027 Advantage plans are still available in our area, the NC mountains.  But all the insurance companies are cutting benefits and increasing out of pocket costs and deductibles by thousands of dollars.  

Most notably to me is our YMCA membership in Spruce Pine, NC which is no longer available through any insurers (that I’m aware of).  We will pay out of pocket for our Y membership next year (about $800 annually for a couple)  because it’s important to me and my wife to stay healthy, and since BCBSNC cut the fitness benefit in 2026 down to Silver Sneakers (which is a joke), we switched to United Healthcare mainly because they covered our Y membership for 2026.  The 2027 United Healthcare’s fitness benefit?  You guessed it… “none”.  The Advantage plans for 2027 remind me of the high deductible plans I had back in the 1980s and 90s when I was self employed.  Essentially catastrophic insurance and that’s all.  

The dental services reimbursements under Advantage plans are ridiculously stingy.  And it’s a crime how all of the insurance companies keep “usual and customary dental fees” a secret.  How in the heck can you compare plans when they won’t say what benchmarks they are using? 

The reason my wife and I chose to go with an Advantage plan is because of the emphasis on staying healthy.  Advantage plans no longer fulfill this purpose…all profit driven.  Health Insurance in the USA is tragic.

comments.body: I agree with many of the commenters here. Devices and screen time are most definitely a huge part of the problem. I would like to see a study of two groups. Group 2: kids who agree not to have devices for a year, and whose parents encourage them to engage in activities outdoors, with their hands, read books, play board games, and interact with their friends in person. Let's then compare results on whatever metrics you like.

comments.name: Mike
comments.body: Excessive screen time does not start at age 9 or 10 (maybe it did when smartphones first started being sold), but within the first few years of a child's life. The false assumption the piece is making, is that mental health problems can be treated at scale directly in kids that have had over a decade of habit forming behaviour. Limiting screen time is a preventative measure that can lead to less children having mental health problems in the first place by changing social norms around screen usage and signalling to parents that there is a problem. Children for whom an intervention like this does not work for should of course get more help, but we cannot expect a system where every single child needs professional care to ever work out.

Awful opinion piece title. More accurate might have been “Child Mental Health Problems Exacerbated by Screens and Social Media”.

About 12 years ago an already challenged young child I knew lost a parent to cancer. The parent understandably decided to pass at home and, ultimately, with hospice assistance. The child witnessing all of it. The surviving parent moved on and extremely fast with a new partner figure. The young child, already confused and in grief, had the arrival of new parent-figure thrown on top of their already emotional & psychological mix. While time did help some, there forward, at age 12 the child received a phone. With no actual oversight and very few limits. Down the rabbit hole that child went with all their unresolved hurt, anxiety, and anger (oh the anger), into a world of teen angst social media. Hour after hour of it and many years, exacerbating pre-existing conditions and to the nines. 

Early on in that child’s phone years, the original surviving parent was questioned about the wisdom of such phone use, to the point of being provided info from early professional studies flashing warning signs. The parent, an otherwise extremely intelligent and capable person, responded “I was on the phone all the time as a teen”. Yeah, in the 1980’s.

comments.name: rolling hills up and down in SF
comments.body:
I read Mamdani’s October 7 statement. Its tone and message overall struck me as appropriate to the situation, of where we were 3 years ago, and where we are today. There’s always going to be something about such statements that “isn’t enough” or “leave out” something that some felt was important, or just wrong. 

Overall, it was fine, given that no matter what he said someone was going to say it wasn’t right. That’s my opinion as a Jew. 

It’s the negative responses that are most interesting to me: they are emblematic of the totality of the conflict itself going back decades, and what we’re living with now. There is always a “but" or “they or didn’t do enough” whatever, or some other bottomless pit of shortcomings and slights and wrongs done by the “others” that just keeps this anger and hate alive. In this instance, we reach the "obscene." 

It’s never going to stop unless we have the courage to step back and understand that the fullness of all the pain felt by everyone can’t be measured, empathized with, or moved on from towards any semblance of peace or justice or order, until we decide to move through it and honestly reach out for any kind of change. And that’s very hard to do that. Mistakes are going to happen & that’s a reality; we have to just let that be & try to help each other do better step by step. There’s no other way at this point because all the blaming accomplishes nothing other than feeding on itself to make sure it never ends.

One would hope on a solemn anniversary, we could all pause and reflect, condemn injustice, and focus on our shared humanity. Our time would be better spent working toward peace, love and understanding, but instead Stephens gives us more outrage. I suppose one could say Mayor Mamdani ruined this year's 9/11 memorial with the release of the long-withheld government records showing that city officials knew the air around Ground Zero was toxic after the September 11, attacks while publicly assuring residents and workers the air was safe. Once again, Mamdani chose to share the truth. We need more truth tellers.

Universities can allow and promote all types of clubs formed around their shared interests, hobbies, and life/career goals, for which each and every student is passionate and can learn, practice, and master desired skill sets, gain new knowledge, expand horizons, and/or possibly meet lifelong friends and build meaningful relationships. 

Fraternities and sororities seem to discourage, if not stop, young, curious minds from wandering around and participating fully in the campus life, exploring diverse opportunities spontaneously, and achieving their full potential through their own initiative and hard work ethic that will fulfill their various needs and important goals. 

College education is like an invitation to an adventure with a map (like the curriculum) and, often, without one, in which case you’re on your own, which is the more challenging and rewarding part of the journey on campus. Quitting fraternities and sororities is like stepping outside the comfort zone and escaping from a well trodden and prescribed path in the woods. You become the trailblazer and change maker. Fear of uncertainty, loneliness, and critical/negative feedback from insiders/peers (old buddies) will become one’s worst enemy. Well, FWIW…

comments.name: Dan Christy
comments.body: I respectfully disagree. I was a member of a fraternity while a student at Purdue in the late sixties and early seventies. We were one of the largest and most diverse of them, while not the most prestigious or influential. I found it provided comaraderie, friendship and yes, brotherhood, instilling values like loyalty, dedication and trust. We had as members the leader of the Students for a Democratic Society ( SDS) and the student commandant of Army ROTC , as wide a split philosophically as you would find in that Vietnam era. ALL agencies can be reformed. Should Christianity be abolished because some clergy are corrupt or evil? All human organizations are subject to abuse. Reform is possible and clearly needed.

This is like saying we should ban any groups of men from congregating. The problem lies with our culture and the conditioning of men, which I wholeheartedly agree with changing. There are also real positives to having actual community and in-person connection in an increasingly isolated society. The sorority I joined at AU truly committed to a zero hazing policy, and we all had A’s as average grades. We pushed each other to be better, not provide some kind of haven for criminal activity as these authors imply.

comments.name: Jon
comments.body:
As an American University alum, I recall that one of the things that drew me to the AU was that Greek life seemed to have a negligible presence on campus. That was decades ago, but I hope it’s still true. 

I understand and share the perspective of the young women who wrote the article, and I admire their effort and persistence. People like them make me hopeful for the future. 

I respectfully disagree on tactics, however. Seeking to ban frats and sororities risks turning allowing those organizations to claim the mantle of beleaguered victims, and to generate sympathy for themselves. 

Instead, I think the anti-Greek movement should follow the path of anti-smoking campaigns: use your social leverage and charisma to gradually persuade more and more young people that Greek Life is pathetic, a bastion for those incapable of making friends on their own, and a cult of those without the character strength to successfully develop as individuals without needing a prefabricated social super-structure.

All of them were significantly riskier than the S&P with beta's ranging from 1.19 to 2.89 with the average beta being 2.07.  Finally, there is a 5% chance of these stocks posting a daily loss of 5.8% with values ranging from 2.7% to 10.1%, a 10% chance of an average daily loss of 9.7% ranging from a low of 4.7% to a high of 14.4% and a 0.1% chance of an average daily loss of 16.3% ranging from a low of 8.1% to a high of 23.0%.  These figures compare to the S&P values of 1.8% with a 5% chance, 3.2% with a 10% chance and 7.3% with a 0.1% chance.

I eventually found out that the family lore was true, my 10th great grandmother, Goodwife Knapp, was hung in what was then Fairfield, CT in 1653,  long before the Salem witch trials. Thirteen in all very accused, the judges were Roger Ludlow (a very prominent name in CT history) and the Reverend Davenport. Goodwife Knapp was hung, cut down and examined for witch marks, then buried in an unmarked grave. There is a monument to her in the vicinity of her hanging. I visited it and left her a white rose. The CT Legislature pardoned all of the accused a few years ago. It was very moving to stand before her monumemt, imagining the terror she must have felt so long ago. Rest in Peace, Goodwife Knapp.

ChatGPT: "If three experts agree with the [best] SI, there isn't even a choice to make. The interesting case is precisely this:
Best SI says A.
Three highly qualified independent experts, with access to the SI's reasoning and evidence, each conclude not-A.

I started as a tenure track faculty member in 1992 and my main task was to start a research program and obtain extramural funding. I was involved with Alzheimer’s research and established a niche being one of the few chemists doing solution NMR with the amyloid peptide that forms amyloid plaques in the brains of individuals with Alzheimer’s.  It was a lot of work but I really enjoyed doing the research with graduate students and grant money was much easier to get back in 90’s when Bill Clinton nearly doubled the NIH budget.

Grant funding has become extremely difficult and sometimes impossible to obtain now and the number of research oriented faculty in universities has declined dramatically in the U.S. over the past 15-years.  I took an early retirement incentive package that was being offered to tenure track faculty and left in 2022 after working for 30-years.  All universities have declined in the hiring of research faculty now, again this is mostly due to lack of government funding.  I still keep in touch with many faculty at my former and other universities and the situation is very sad.

I worked as a young engineer for GE's Valley Forge Space Division near Philadelphia in the mid-70s, where I learned that from time to time we had freeze-dried books that had been soaked in water during some natural disaster to rescue them. I can only recall that we did it for a very, very prominent library. 

We used a large environmental test chamber (ordinarily reserved for testing the satellites we designed, developed, and built there) that could pull a vacuum equivalent to outer space while simultaneously lowering the temperature to well below freezing. The process was quite successful in rescuing the books, but very time consuming to do and not at all economically viable for the volume of books that needed the time-critical treatment; wet books deteriorate quickly.

The process involved some additional chemical(s) intended to keep pages from sticking after drying. 

I often wonder if the freeze-drying process might now be a viable method of rescuing damaged books.

Their priority is to find a home for the child, and they are not going to remove him from a home once they have found one, particularly if the parents deny the severity of his behavior. I think it is also important to recognize that neurological and psychological development and behavioral issues are well documented in children who have been exposed to drug abuse/alcohol abuse while in the womb. This is not some woke or liberal thing. It is quality peer reviewed science. 

Fetal Alcohol Syndrome, Neonatal Abstinence syndrome, Fetal Drug Syndromes are all real. Add that in to an environment that is negligent, unstable, perhaps physically abusive, and certainly psychologically abusive and negligent and it is a mess.

These are serious medical and neuropsychiatric issues which must be addressed. There has been a great deal of study and experience over the last several decades and the resources are valuable.

He thought it was funny. I took my son aside and told him politely but strongly the problem was not just the child's behavior but the failure of he and his wife to recognize that this child needed help and intervention and far better guidance and training.  
Even at pre school the parents were told "your son has a behavior problem". One school would no longer accept him.  So, finally at about age 4-5 the parents started to seek help.  
Initially my son and his wife were very annoyed that I "butted in".  But, eventually they recognized that they were part of the problem. Even when things are his he learned to calm down and not be destructive. It took both parents and professional help to get this kids straightened out.  
I was in the dog house for a while but I was wiling to accept that in order to get the message to my son and daughter-in-law.

comments.name: Foster Parent
comments.body:
This advice seems well intentioned but unaware of best practices. Children experiencing foster care - from newborns to teens - have experienced trauma. Parenting a child who’s experienced trauma will look different than the parenting many of us experienced. This does not mean that challenging behaviors should be ignored or dismissed. Rather, it means that interventions must be used intentionally and often only when the child is regulated. It’s likely that the concerned sister is not able to see everything that is happening to support this child so they can learn healthier behaviors. 

My advice would be for the concerned sister to learn more about trauma-informed parenting, listen to former foster youth about their experiences, and offer more support to the foster parents so they can best meet the needs of the child. This might include reading books about any diagnoses the child has been given (if the foster parents are able to share), signing up to be a respite provider, or offering support in the form of laundry, meal prep, etc. They could also search out content creators of former foster youth or other foster parents so they can see what best helps youth of all ages who are growing up after experiencing trauma.

We can ALL show up to support kids who’ve experienced trauma and/or foster care even if we can’t all be foster parents.

comments.body:
The American Disability Act (ADA) of 1990, and as amended in 2010 addresses this issue.  

That act specifically doesn't allow for existing buildings to be "grandfathered" in.  

Just on what you said, it seems that your building did attempt to comply with the code.  Which is why there are handicapped spaces to begin with.  The ADA violation may be that the building sold those spaces, and they are no longer accessible.  Selling those spaces to individual non-handicapped individuals was and is likely illegal.  

So, I'd start with having my attorney writing a letter the Owner of the building, and the HOA.   In that letter, identify the ADA violation(s), and ask what steps are being taken to comply with Federal Law.  Everything you need to do this is available at ada.com.

My gut feeling is that this is a Building Owner issue.  I'm guessing they submitted plans in compliance with the ADA, but then violated that compliance by selling the accessible parking spaces.  No bueno.

I'd also file a complaint with the ADA.  You can do it online.  I'd start with that.  Include a copy of your ADA complaint with your letter to the building owner and HOA.

You absolutely have action here, imo.  And you're asking the right questions.

If the parking space were not actually conveyed to unit owners, the unit owners will likely have easement rights in the parking areas (along with the other common areas) and spaces are assigned/allocated by the Condo Board. A review of the other condo docs would then be in order.

comments.name: Ben
comments.body:
This advice seems to overlook the most fundamental legal question: who actually owns the parking spaces?

At least on the West Coast, it’s not unusual for condominium parking spaces to be independently deeded units of real estate, rather than common property administered by the HOA. Once lawfully created and sold, those units belong to their individual owners. The HOA has no more authority to reassign them than it does to reassign someone’s apartment.

Nor does accessible striping on the pavement necessarily establish a continuing legal restriction. Markings can remain from the building’s original construction even when the underlying property has subsequently been conveyed into private ownership.

Both the article and many of these comments seem to conflate apartment buildings operated by landlords with privately owned condominium developments governed by associations of the owners themselves. An HOA is not a landlord. It cannot simply redistribute privately owned real estate to satisfy another resident’s needs.

If the building was lawfully developed, all parking was sold into private ownership, and the association retains no common parking or reassignment authority, what exactly is it legally obligated or even empowered to provide?

The article seems to skip that threshold question entirely.  Seems to me that’s a remarkable omission in a real estate advice column.

comments.name: FromBK2LA

Generally speaking, from the perspective of a non-disabled layman, I often see people pulling into these spots in expensive sports cars, getting out with ease, and walking away without any apparent mobility issues. It naturally raises questions about whether the system is being abused.

When I was younger, I generally observed these parking spots utilized only by people in wheelchairs or those with obvious mobility limitations. Today, at least from what I observe in my own bubble, that visual is rarely the case.

That said, not all disabilities are visible, and someone's ability to walk doesn't necessarily reflect their need for accessible parking. So, who am I to judge someone else's disability based solely on what I can observe?

Do we need better metrics to determine who is disabled enough to qualify for these spots? Probably. But those determinations should be based on legitimate medical needs rather than appearances or assumptions.

The vast majority of Indians support the government, and allegations such as “vote theft” need to be backed by credible evidence, not amplified through political theatrics and social media spectacles. The protests have increasingly become a meme factory, and the more they descend into theatrics, the more they risk alienating ordinary Indians and strengthening support for the BJP.

The fact that dissent is visible and vocal is itself relevant to the debate about Indian democracy. Democratic freedoms do not, however, grant protesters a free pass for hooliganism or disorder.

From a layperson's perspective, they both seem to be downstream artifacts and not causal.  I'd love to see more studies linking insulin resistance and poor metabolic health with both AD other dementias. Excited about the prospect of emerging multi-targeted biologics, GLP-1 receptor agonists to improve brain insulin signaling, CRISPER, glymphatic function optimization, and other treatments on the horizon.

comments.body: I wonder whether we’re focusing too much on the plaques and tangles and not enough on what causes them to accumulate in the first place. What if Alzheimer’s begins, at least in part, with a failure of the brain’s glymphatic system to clear metabolic waste? Amyloid and tau could be downstream consequences that then accelerate the damage, while genetic predispositions determine how quickly the process unfolds. Like a beaver building a dam, the accumulation becomes destructive, but removing the dam doesn't necessarily fix the conditions that allowed it to form. Perhaps we should be looking further upstream.

A dear friend of mine is entering the late stages of Alzheimer’s disease at only 68.  The symptoms have accelerated quickly over the past two months to the point where he is now in a memory care unit and declining rapidly.  That said, he was one of the first people to be treated with one of the new anti-amyloid drugs due to his wife’s persistence with his insurance company. Tragically for him, it did nothing to help even though it reportedly worked at clearing the plaques.  It did cause brain swelling and some bleeding, with requisite pauses in treatments.  I remember reading about these new drugs and discovering that, even in trials, there was little to no effect on the disease’s progression.  How these types of drugs managed to get approval with essentially no benefits - but plenty of costs - speaks a lot to the state of our corporate- and profit-driven health care system as well as the willingness of people to grasp whatever hope they can.

He was a brilliant biologist and has been a great friend since we were adolescents.  I already miss him, but pray for him to be a peace soon.  I also pray that research will find a way to halt or cure this awful disease without generating false hope.

comments.name: Matt
comments.body:
Let me transgress, a literary term I picked up a few years ago, as part of a sometimes confusing effort to be a better writer, and admit to a few things.
I’m guessing I’m not the only one who has no time to read books, not that I don’t regret that, and count on Reviews to at least give me a taste of aspects of life I would otherwise totally miss.
I suspect that if I did attempt to read this one, there are so many things going on, some of which I would miss, I would either drop it, or resort to a strategy I sometimes use in dealing with non-literary complex matters. That is, just enjoy the parts you get, while acknowledging there is more out there.
So thanks to the reviewer for both explaining how writing can show both what is and isn’t obvious. 
That ability, I find, has good, if undertapped utility in life.
And for helping to explain another subject I’ve found confusing, in part because the rules keep changing; that is, what is good writing.
With character limits approaching, just two more thoughts.
I write this, in part, because there are currently zero comments. That is disrespectful to the reviewer and to the author.
Finally, as I note the reviewer is a professor at Rutgers, presumedly in the English Department, I hope he takes this message back, as I had my freshman writing class there in 1973.
It isn’t often that a student complains about getting an “A.” It was giddy finding out I was better than I thought.
But I really wasn’t. And paid for it.
I hope it’s better now.
